To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the resting state network connectivity is altered in altered state of consciousness; 2) the alterations are consistent across physiological (sleep), pathological (vegetative state/unresponsive-wakefulness syndrome, coma, brain death, minimally conscious state) and pharmacological (general anesthesia) altered states of consciousness; 3) the alterations are mainly decreases of functional connectivity between brain regions belonging to the default-mode network and increases of functional connectivity between sensorimotor and auditory/visual networks; 4
resting state networks are not a unitary phenomenon but are rather a dynamic network of networks that are differentially modulated in physiological, pharmacologically and pathological altered states.
“The DMN, the salience, executive control and sensorimotor networks are consistently altered in altered states of consciousness”.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the functional organization of the brain, and the conscious processes that are associated with it.
the neural basis of consciousness and its alteration in physiological and pathological conditions.
the functional connectivity of the brain during resting state.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the functional contribution of RSNs to consciousness is complex, multifaceted, and still not well understood.
the DMN and executive control networks are necessary for conscious cognition and that the salience network is sufficient to sustain consciousness.
the resting state networks are altered in all physiological and pathological conditions of consciousness.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the resting state network connectivity is altered in all the studied altered states of consciousness.
the functional connectivity of the resting state networks is a promising tool for the study of consciousness.
the DMN is a necessary but not sufficient condition for conscious cognition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the resting state approach can help us understand the neural correlates of conscious processes and the mechanisms that underlie the transition from unconsciousness to consciousness.

resting state connectivity can be used as an index of the integrity of the neural networks that underlie consciousness, and that it can help us understand the neural correlates of conscious cognition.
